argument_summary: The admissible record supports certification only in a caveated form. Aggregate readiness is above threshold, launch rehearsal showed no severity-one incidents, and general support, latency, and rollback checks passed for the launch configuration. The same admissible record also shows that those checks do not cover high-risk reset request routing, that this is a named deployment context, and that its dedicated evals are not in the packet. On that evidence, the defensible position is not clean certification of the named context; it is certification with an explicit recorded limitation that named-context coverage remains incomplete.
claims_about_business_cost: No independent business-cost claim is needed to justify the policy position. The admissible basis is that caveated certification preserves the readiness signal already established by aggregate and operational evidence without overstating support for the uncovered named context.
claims_about_policy: The governing policy cuts against clean certification, not against all certification. The policy text says material limitations and evaluation gaps for named deployment contexts must be disclosed, and that passing general benchmarks and load tests can support launch readiness but do not substitute for missing named-context coverage. That means the compliant reading of the current packet is caveated compliance if the certification record expressly states the gap, not noncompliance per se and not clean compliance.
concessions: There is no admissible evidence here showing the actual certification artifact already contains the required disclosure text.
There is no admissible evidence that high-risk reset request routing has completed dedicated evaluations.
General readiness and operational-pass evidence do not establish support for the uncovered named high-risk context.
The draft model-card statement that there are no known password recovery limitations is too broad on this record because QA treats the missing evals as unknown, not passed.
